paragraphs: Poseidon helps the Achaeans—The feats of Idomeneus—Hector at the ships.

Now that Zeus had brought Hector and the Trojans to the ships, he left them to their endless toil. He turned his keen eyes away and looked elsewhere, toward the horse-breeders of Thrace, the Mysians who fight at close quarters, the noble Hippemolgi who live on milk, and the Abians, the most just of mankind. He no longer cast even a glance toward Troy. He did not think that any of the immortals would go to help either the Trojans or the Danaans.

But King Poseidon had not been keeping a careless watch. He sat on the highest peaks of wooded Samothrace and gazed at the battle in admiration. From there he could see all of Ida, with the city of Priam and the ships of the Achaeans. He had come up from under the sea to take this seat, because he pitied the Achaeans, who were being beaten by the Trojans, and he was furiously angry with Zeus.

Soon he left his post on the mountaintop. He strode swiftly on, and the high hills and the forest shook under his immortal feet. He took three strides, and with the fourth he reached his destination, Aegae, where his glittering golden palace stands in the depths of the sea, never to decay. When he arrived, he harnessed his swift bronze-footed horses, whose golden manes streamed in the wind. He put on clothing of gold, took up his golden whip, and stepped onto his chariot. As he drove out over the waves, the sea monsters left their lairs, for they knew their lord. They came playing around him from every part of the deep, and the sea in her gladness opened a path for his chariot. The horses flew so lightly that the bronze axle of the car stayed dry beneath it. In this way his bounding horses carried him to the ships of the Achaeans.

In the depths of the sea, midway between Tenedos and rocky Imbrus, there is a huge cavern. Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, stopped his horses there, unyoked them, and set ambrosial fodder before them. He tied their feet with golden hobbles that no one could loosen or break, so that they would stay in that place until their lord came back. Then he went on to the army of the Achaeans.

The Trojans were following Hector son of Priam in close formation, like a storm cloud or a blaze of fire. They fought with all their strength and raised the battle cry, for they believed they would take the ships of the Achaeans and kill all their greatest heroes then and there. Meanwhile earth-encircling Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, was encouraging the Argives. He had come up out of the sea and taken the form and voice of Calchas.

He spoke first to the two Ajaxes, who were already doing their best. “Ajaxes,” he said, “you two can save the Achaeans, if you give all your strength and refuse to be frightened. I am not afraid for any other part of the line, though the Trojans have crossed the wall in force. The Achaeans can hold them all back there. But I fear greatly that some evil will fall on us here, where furious Hector is leading them on like a pillar of flame. He boasts that he is the son of great Zeus himself. May some god put it into your hearts to make a firm stand here and to urge others to do the same. Then you will drive him from the ships, even if Zeus himself inspires him.”

As he spoke, the earth-encircling lord of the earthquake struck them both with his scepter and filled their hearts with courage. He made their legs light and quick, and their hands and feet as well. Then, as a soaring falcon hovers on the wing high above a sheer rock and soon swoops down to chase a bird over the plain, so Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, took wing into the air and left them. Swift Ajax son of Oileus was the first of the two to realize who had been speaking with them. He said to Ajax son of Telamon, “Ajax, this is one of the gods who live on Olympus. He has taken the likeness of the prophet to tell us to fight hard by our ships. It was not Calchas, the seer and reader of omens. I knew him at once by his feet and knees as he turned away, for gods are easily recognized. And I feel the lust for battle burning more fiercely inside me, while my hands and feet beneath me are more eager for the fight.”
Ajax son of Telamon answered, “I feel it too. My hands grip my spear more firmly, my strength is greater, and my feet are quicker. I even long to meet furious Hector son of Priam in single combat.”

So they talked, delighting in the hunger for battle that the god had put into them. Meanwhile the earth-encircler stirred up the Achaeans who were resting in the rear by the ships. They were worn out at once by hard fighting and by grief at seeing that the Trojans had crossed the wall in force. Tears fell from their eyes as they watched, for they were sure they would not escape destruction. But the lord of the earthquake moved lightly among them and drove their battalions to the front.

He went first to Teucer and Leitus, the hero Peneleos, Thoas and Deipyrus, and Meriones and Antilochus, valiant warriors. He urged them all on. “Shame on you, young Argives,” he cried. “I relied on your prowess to save our ships. If you do not fight with all your strength, this very day will see us beaten by the Trojans. I truly see with my own eyes a great and terrible portent that I never thought I would see: Trojans at our ships! They used to be like panic-stricken deer in a forest, prey for jackals and wolves, with no strength except in flight, since they cannot defend themselves. Until now the Trojans did not dare face the attack of the Achaeans for a single moment. Now they have come far out from their city and are fighting at our very ships, because of our leader’s cowardice and the disaffection of the people themselves. In their discontent they do not care to fight in defense of the ships, and they are being slaughtered beside them. It is true that King Agamemnon son of Atreus is the cause of our disaster, because he insulted the son of Peleus. Still, that is no reason for us to stop fighting. Let us be quick to heal, for the hearts of the brave heal quickly. You do wrong to be so slack, you who are the finest soldiers in our whole army. I do not blame a man for staying out of battle if he is a weakling, but I am angry with men like you. My good friends, this slackness will soon make matters even worse. Each of you, think of your own honor and reputation, for the danger of the fight is extreme. Great Hector is now fighting at our ships. He has broken through the gates and the strong bolt that held them.”

So the earth-encircler addressed the Achaeans and urged them on. Strong bands of men gathered around the two Ajaxes. Not even Ares, or Athena who marshals the hosts, could have made light of them had they gone among them, for these were the picked men of all who were waiting for the attack of Hector and the Trojans. They made a living fence, spear to spear, shield to shield, buckler to buckler, helmet to helmet, and man to man. The horsehair crests on their gleaming helmets touched as they nodded forward, so close were they packed. The spears in their strong hands were interlaced, and their hearts were set on battle.

The Trojans advanced in a dense body, with Hector at their head pressing straight on, like a rock that comes thundering down a mountainside after winter torrents have torn it from the brow. Floods of rain have loosened the foundations of the dull thing, and as it bounds headlong on its way it sets the whole forest roaring. It swerves neither right nor left until it reaches level ground, but there, for all its fury, it can go no further. In the same way Hector for a while seemed as though he would rampage through the tents and ships of the Achaeans, slaughtering as he went, until he reached the sea. But the closely packed battalions stopped him when he reached them. The sons of the Achaeans thrust at him with swords and with spears pointed at both ends, and drove him back so that he staggered and gave ground. Then he shouted to the Trojans, “Trojans, Lycians, and Dardanians, fighters in close combat, stand firm! The Achaeans have set themselves up as a wall against me, but they will not hold me for long. They will give way before me, if the mightiest of the gods, the thundering husband of Hera, has truly inspired my attack.”

With these words he put heart and soul into them all. Deiphobus son of Priam went among them, intent on deeds of daring. He held his round shield before him and strode quickly forward under its cover. Meriones took aim at him with a spear and did not miss, hitting the broad circle of ox-hide. But he was far from piercing it. The spear broke in two long before it could, and Deiphobus had also seen it coming and held his shield well away from him. Meriones drew back among his comrades, angry both at failing to defeat Deiphobus and at breaking his spear. So he turned toward the ships and tents to fetch a spear he had left behind in his tent.

The others went on fighting, and the cry of battle rose to the heavens. Teucer son of Telamon was the first to kill his man, the warrior Imbrius, son of Mentor, rich in horses. Until the Achaeans came, Imbrius had lived in Pedaeum and had married Medesicaste, a bastard daughter of Priam. When the Danaan fleet arrived, he went back to Ilium. He became a great man among the Trojans and lived near Priam himself, who gave him the same honor as his own sons. Now the son of Telamon struck him with a spear under the ear, then drew it back out. Imbrius fell headlong, like an ash tree felled on the crest of a high mountain beacon, when its delicate green foliage comes toppling to the ground. So he fell, with his bronze-wrought armor ringing harshly around him. Teucer sprang forward, meaning to strip off his armor, but as he did, Hector took aim at him with a spear. Teucer saw it coming and swerved aside. The spear hit Amphimachus, son of Cteatus son of Actor, in the chest as he was coming into the battle, and his armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground. Hector sprang forward to pull the helmet from Amphimachus’s temples. At once Ajax threw a spear at him but did not wound him, because he was covered all over in his terrible armor. Still, the spear struck the boss of his shield with such force that it drove him back from the two corpses, and the Achaeans pulled them away. Stichius and Menestheus, captains of the Athenians, carried Amphimachus to the host of the Achaeans, while the two brave and impetuous Ajaxes did the same for Imbrius. As when two lions snatch a goat from hounds that have it in their fangs and carry it in their jaws, high off the ground, through thick brushwood, so the Ajaxes carried Imbrius’s body aloft and stripped off its armor. Then the son of Oileus, in revenge for the death of Amphimachus, cut the head from the neck and sent it whirling through the crowd like a ball, until it fell in the dust at Hector’s feet.

Poseidon was furiously angry that his grandson Amphimachus had fallen. He went to the tents and ships of the Achaeans to urge the Danaans on still further and to plan trouble for the Trojans. Idomeneus met him as he was leaving a comrade who had just come from the fight, wounded in the knee. His fellow soldiers had carried the man off the field. Idomeneus gave orders to the physicians and went on to his tent, for he was still thirsting for battle. Poseidon spoke in the likeness and with the voice of Thoas son of Andraemon, who ruled the Aetolians of all Pleuron and high Calydon and was honored among his people as if he were a god. “Idomeneus,” he said, “lawgiver to the Cretans, what has become of the threats the sons of the Achaeans used to make against the Trojans?”

Idomeneus, chief among the Cretans, answered, “Thoas, as far as I know, no one is at fault, for we can all fight. Neither fear nor slackness holds anyone back. It seems to be the will of almighty Zeus that the Achaeans should perish without glory here, far from Argos. You, Thoas, have always been staunch, and you keep others in heart when you see anyone fail in duty. So do not be slack now, but urge everyone to do his utmost.”

Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, answered him, “Idomeneus, may the man who is slack in fighting this day by his own choice never return from Troy, but stay here for the dogs to feast on. Get your armor and come. We must hurry together, if we can be of any use, though we are only two. Even cowards gain courage from company, and we two can hold our own against the bravest.”

With that the god went back into the thick of the fight. Idomeneus reached his tent, put on his armor, took up his two spears, and rushed out. His armor gleamed about him as he ran, like the lightning that the son of Cronus brandishes from bright Olympus when he wants to show a sign to mortals, and its flash shines far and wide. His sturdy squire Meriones met him while he was still near his tent (Meriones was going to fetch his spear), and Idomeneus said:

“Meriones, swift son of Molus, best of comrades, why did you leave the fight? Has a weapon’s point wounded you and left you in pain? Or did someone send you to bring me back? I need no one to bring me. I would much prefer to fight than stay in my tent.”
“Idomeneus,” Meriones answered, “I have come for a spear, if I can find one in my tent. I broke the one I had when I threw it at the shield of Deiphobus.”

Idomeneus, captain of the Cretans, answered, “If you want one spear, or twenty, you will find them standing against the end wall of my tent. I took them from Trojans I have killed, for I do not keep my enemy at arm’s length. That is why I have spears, bossed shields, helmets, and burnished corslets.”

Then Meriones said, “I also have spoils taken from the Trojans, in my tent and at my ship, but they are not at hand. I have always been brave, and wherever the fighting was hard I have held my own among the foremost. There may be Achaeans who do not know how I fight, but you know it well enough yourself.”

Idomeneus answered, “I know you are a brave man, and you need not tell me. Suppose the best men at the ships were being chosen for an ambush—nothing shows what a man is made of like that, for it comes out then who is a coward and who is brave. The coward changes color at every turn. He is full of fear and keeps shifting his weight, first on one knee and then on the other. His heart beats fast as he thinks of death, and you can hear his teeth chattering. The brave man does not change color or take fright on finding himself in ambush, but longs the whole time to go into action. If the best men were being chosen for such a service, no one could make light of your courage or your feats of arms. If you were hit by a dart or struck in close combat, it would not be from behind, in your neck or back. The weapon would hit you in the chest or belly as you pressed forward to a place in the front ranks. But let us stop standing here talking like children, or we will be spoken ill of. Go and fetch your spear from the tent at once.”

At this, Meriones, the equal of Ares, went to the tent and got himself a bronze spear. He followed after Idomeneus, set on great deeds of valor. As when baneful Ares goes out to battle, and his son Panic, strong and dauntless, goes with him to strike terror even into the heart of a hero—the pair have left Thrace to arm themselves among the Ephyri or the brave Phlegyans, but they will not listen to both of the contending armies, and will give victory to one side or the other—so Meriones and Idomeneus, captains of men, went out to battle in their bronze armor. Meriones spoke first. “Son of Deucalion,” he said, “where would you have us begin fighting? On the right wing of the army, in the center, or on the left wing, where I think the Achaeans will be weakest?”

Idomeneus answered, “There are others to defend the center: the two Ajaxes and Teucer, the finest archer of all the Achaeans and good in a hand-to-hand fight too. They will give Hector son of Priam all he can handle. Fight as he may, he will find it hard to overcome their indomitable fury and set fire to the ships, unless the son of Cronus hurls a firebrand on them with his own hand. Great Ajax son of Telamon will yield to no man who is of mortal mold and eats the grain of Demeter, so long as bronze and great stones can bring him down. He would not give way even to Achilles in hand-to-hand fighting, and in speed of foot no one can beat him. So let us turn toward the left wing, and find out at once whether we will give glory to someone else, or he to us.”
Meriones, the equal of swift Ares, then led the way until they came to the part of the army that Idomeneus had named.

When the Trojans saw Idomeneus coming at them like a flame of fire, he and his squire in their richly wrought armor, they shouted and moved against him all together. A furious hand-to-hand fight raged beside the ships’ sterns. The fury of the combat was like the shrill winds that whistle on a day when dust lies deep on the roads and the gusts raise it in a thick cloud. With all their might they hacked at each other with spear and sword throughout the army. The field bristled with the long, deadly spears they carried. The sheen of their gleaming helmets, their freshly burnished breastplates, and their glittering shields was dazzling as they joined battle. His courage must be iron indeed who could take pleasure in the sight of such turmoil and look on it without dismay.

So the two mighty sons of Cronus plotted evil for mortal heroes. Zeus meant to give victory to the Trojans and to Hector, to honor swift-footed Achilles. Yet he did not mean to destroy the Achaean army utterly before Ilium. He only wanted to glorify Thetis and her valiant son. Poseidon, on the other hand, went among the Argives to urge them on. He had come up from the gray sea in secret, because he was grieved to see them beaten by the Trojans and was furiously angry with Zeus. The two gods shared the same race and country, but Zeus was born first and knew more. So Poseidon was afraid to defend the Argives openly. In the likeness of a man, he kept encouraging them throughout their army. In this way the two gods tied a knot of war and battle that no one could undo or break, and set both sides tugging at it, until the men’s knees failed beneath them.

Now Idomeneus, though his hair was already flecked with gray, called loudly to the Danaans and spread panic among the Trojans as he leaped in among them. He killed Othryoneus of Cabesus, a visitor who had only lately come to join the war. Othryoneus had sought Cassandra, the fairest of Priam’s daughters, in marriage, but offered no gifts of wooing. He promised something great instead: that he would drive the sons of the Achaeans from Troy, whether they liked it or not. Old King Priam had agreed and promised her to him, and Othryoneus fought on the strength of those promises. Idomeneus aimed a spear and hit him as he came striding on. His bronze cuirass did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly, so that he fell heavily to the ground. Then Idomeneus boasted over him. “Othryoneus,” he said, “there is no one in the world I will admire more than you, if you really do what you promised Priam son of Dardanus in return for his daughter. We also will make you an offer. We will give you the loveliest daughter of the son of Atreus and bring her from Argos for you to marry, if you will sack the goodly city of Ilium with us. So come along with me, and we will make a covenant about the marriage at the ships. We will not be hard on you about gifts of wooing.”

With this Idomeneus began dragging him by the foot through the thick of the fight. But Asius came up to protect the body, on foot, in front of his horses. His squire drove them so close behind him that he could feel their breath on his shoulder. Asius longed to strike Idomeneus down, but before he could, Idomeneus struck him with his spear in the throat under the chin, and the bronze point went clean through. He fell like an oak, a poplar, or a pine that shipwrights have felled on the mountains with whetted axes for ship’s timber. So he lay at full length in front of his chariot and horses, grinding his teeth and clutching at the blood-stained dust. His charioteer was struck with panic. He did not dare turn his horses around and escape. Then Antilochus hit him in the middle of his body with a spear. His bronze cuirass did not protect him, and the spear stuck in his belly. He fell gasping from his chariot, and Antilochus, great Nestor’s son, drove his horses away from the Trojans to the Achaeans.

Deiphobus then came close to Idomeneus to avenge Asius and aimed a spear at him. But Idomeneus was on the lookout and dodged it, covered by the round shield he always carried—a shield of ox-hide and bronze with two arm-rods on the inside. He crouched under it, and the spear flew over him. The shield rang out as the spear grazed it, yet the weapon did not leave the strong hand of Deiphobus in vain. It struck Hypsenor son of Hippasus, shepherd of his people, in the liver under the midriff, and his limbs gave way beneath him. Deiphobus boasted over him and cried out in a loud voice, “Truly, Asius has not fallen unavenged. He will be glad even as he passes into the house of Hades, the strong gatekeeper, that I have sent someone to escort him.”

So he boasted, and the Argives were stung by his words. Noble Antilochus was angrier than anyone, but grief did not make him forget his friend and comrade. He ran to him, stood over him, and covered him with his shield. Then two of his staunch comrades, Mecisteus son of Echius and Alastor, stooped down and carried him groaning heavily to the ships. But Idomeneus did not ease his fury. He kept striving, again and again, either to wrap some Trojan in the darkness of death, or to fall himself while warding off the evil day from the Achaeans. Then Alcathous fell, son of noble Aesyetes. He was son-in-law to Anchises, having married his eldest daughter Hippodameia. She was the darling of her father and mother and surpassed all her generation in beauty, accomplishments, and understanding, and so the bravest man in all Troy had taken her as his wife. Poseidon laid this man low by the hand of Idomeneus. He blinded his bright eyes and bound his strong limbs in fetters, so that Alcathous could neither go back nor step aside, but stood stock still like a pillar or a lofty tree when Idomeneus struck him with a spear in the middle of his chest. The coat of mail that had protected his body until then was broken, and it rang harshly as the spear tore through it. He fell heavily to the ground, and the spear stuck in his heart. The heart still beat, and made the butt-end of the spear quiver, until dread Ares put an end to his life. Idomeneus boasted over him and cried out in a loud voice, “Deiphobus, since you are in the mood to boast, shall we call it even now that we have killed three men to your one? No, sir, stand and fight me yourself, so that you learn what kind of man I am, born of Zeus, who have come here. Zeus first fathered Minos, chief ruler in Crete, and Minos in his turn fathered a son, noble Deucalion. Deucalion fathered me to rule over many men in Crete, and now my ships have brought me here to be the bane of you, your father, and the Trojans.”
